title: Gold loan growth slows as falling gold prices push lenders into collection mode - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
The correction has left several lenders grappling with elevated risk levels

Gold loan companies are shifting their focus from growth to collections after a sharp fall in gold prices pushed loan-to-value (LTV) ratios higher across the industry, raising concerns over margin breaches and future asset quality stress.

Industry executives said portfolio-level LTVs have climbed well above the levels seen earlier this year, as gold prices corrected nearly 19 per cent from their January peaks. The rise comes after lenders expanded aggressively during the gold rally, with major gold financiers reporting over 60 per cent year-on-year loan growth in the September quarter.

The correction has left several lenders grappling with elevated risk levels. Portfolio LTVs at some gold-loan-focused NBFCs have crossed 75 per cent, while certain segments may have breached 85 per cent following the sharp decline in collateral values, executives said. Loans originated at 80-85 per cent LTV after the RBI relaxed norms for lower-ticket loans have seen ratios jump to 90-95 per cent after the recent correction in gold prices.

The immediate response from lenders has been to tighten collections.

“My full effort right now is into collections. Growth is not happening. In November, I am not focused on growth at all. The focus is reducing the LTV and collections,” a senior executive at a leading gold-loan company said.

Another industry executive said the stress is visible across the sector. “Stress is definitely there because everybody is focusing more on collection rather than business,” the executive said, adding that lenders are increasingly seeking additional margins and collateral from borrowers.

Companies have also started offering interest-rate rebates and other incentives to ensure borrowers continue servicing their loans. Executives said many customers are being asked either to repay a portion of their loans or pledge additional gold as collateral to restore regulatory and internal LTV thresholds.

Parth Gutka of 360 ONE Capital, said the impact of higher LTVs is likely to emerge in asset quality metrics over the next few quarters. “Loans that originated at over 60 per cent LTV have now reached 75 per cent and this would roughly be half of the overall gold loan portfolio,” Gutka said. He added that NBFCs remain more vulnerable than banks because banks have generally been more conservative in their gold-loan underwriting.

Piran Engineer, Senior Research Analyst at CLSA India, said stress could start surfacing as early as the December quarter, with lenders increasingly demanding additional collateral and repayments to maintain adequate coverage.

Analysts expect the industry’s breakneck growth to moderate sharply as companies prioritise safeguarding collateral values over building their loan books. “Gold business in terms of growth will definitely slow down. From last two years, what percentage we have seen, I am sure this year we will not see that kind of growth,” an industry executive said.

While some industry participants are hopeful of a recovery in gold prices after December, executives said the near-term focus will remain firmly on collections and risk management, with fresh business taking a back seat until collateral values stabilise.
